==English==

===Etymology===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:angry|tree=1}}
From {{der|en|enm|angry}}, equivalent to {{af|en|anger|-y|id2=adjectival}}; see {{m|en|anger}}.

===Adjective===
{{wikidata lexeme|L3246}}
{{en-adj|er,more}}

# Displaying or feeling [[anger]].
#: {{ux|en|His face became '''angry'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|An '''angry''' mob started looting the warehouse.}}
#* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=5|passage=Then we relapsed into a discomfited silence, and wished we were anywhere else. But Miss Thorn relieved the situation by laughing aloud, and with such a hearty enjoyment that instead of getting '''angry''' and more mortified we began to laugh ourselves, and instantly felt better.}}
#* {{RQ:en:CNN|author=John Blake|title=Remembering the theologian who took on the hypocrisy of the white church|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/04/30/us/remembering-theologian-james-cone|date=2018-04-30|passage=Cone, who once called himself “the '''angriest''' theologian in America,” is still '''angry'''.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20250821204458/https://www.cnn.com/2018/04/30/us/remembering-theologian-james-cone}}
#* {{RQ:en:CNN|author=Thomas Lake|title=17 years later, I still remember this act of kindness from another driver|url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/06/10/us/driving-courtesy-highway-19-florida-stranger-cec|date=2024-06-10|passage=I kept my window rolled up, eyes on the road, probably making the pickup man '''angrier''' with my silence.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20240613034639/https://www.cnn.com/2024/06/10/us/driving-courtesy-highway-19-florida-stranger-cec/}}

But it isn’t always useful, Romanoff said.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20250614213800/https://www.cnn.com/2025/05/16/health/going-to-bed-angry-bad-advice-wellness}}
# {{lb|en|said about a wound or a rash}} {{cap|inflamed}} and [[painful]].
#: {{ux|en|The broken glass left two '''angry''' cuts across my arm.}}
# {{lb|en|figuratively|said about the elements, like the sky or the sea}} Dark and stormy, [[menacing]].
#: {{ux|en|'''Angry''' clouds raced across the sky.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1756|author=w:Christopher Smart|title=[http://books.google.com/books?id=fnpYmCFiZlcC The Book of the Epodes]|chapter=Ode II|by=w:Horace
|passage={{...}}nor dreads he the '''angry''' sea{{...}}}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1997|author=Kelly Joyce Neff|title=Dear Companion: The Inner Life of Martha Jefferson|page=92
|passage=When she and her sister were away at Williamsburg, Nancy and I were more like founderers on a raft adrift in an '''angry''' sea.}}

====Usage notes====
* The comparative '''more angry''' and the superlative '''most angry''' are also occasionally found.

* The sense “feeling anger” is construed with {{m|en|with}} or {{m|en|at}} when the object is a person: ''I’m angry with/at my boss.'' It is construed with {{m|en|at}} or {{m|en|about}} when the object is a situation: ''I’m angry at/about what he said''. When both a person and a situation are given, the latter is construed with {{m|en|for}} instead: ''I’m angry with/at my boss for what he said.'' But, as with many other words for emotions, sentences with an unmarked subordinate clause are also possible: ''Are you angry I'm here with you?''

====Synonyms====
* {{sense|displaying anger}} [[upset]], {{l|en|mad}}, {{l|en|enraged}}, {{l|en|wrathful}}, {{l|en|furious}}, {{l|en|apoplectic}}; [[irritated]], [[annoyed]], [[vexed]], [[pissed off]], [[cheesed off]], [[worked up]], [[psyched up]], [[ireful]].
* See also [[Thesaurus:angry]]

===Noun===
{{en-noun}}

# {{lb|en|informal|rare}} An [[#Adjective|angry]] person.
#* {{quote-newsgroup|en|date=16 November 2001|author=Lenny Stover|quotee=Harry T. O'Reilly|title=ONLY A COP|newsgroup=alt.law-enforcement|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20260412174931/https://groups.google.com/g/alt.law-enforcement/c/0yJK4v1YxFg/m/yjZykgJ2SgYJ|passage=He knows the young buffalos who bitch beyond reasonable bitching but still do the job, and he knows the '''angries''', the men who never seem to feel good about themselves because of the seemingly endless struggle against an unrealistic bureaucracy that demands so much of them and offers so little in the way of reward or compensation. After all, they are "only" cops.}}
#* {{quote-newsgroup|en|date=24 December 2003|author=SteveR|title=U.S. Recovery? Tell It to the Unemployed|newsgroup=austin.general|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20260412174143/https://groups.google.com/g/austin.general/c/VMF3yK0OB68/m/m3fB0Fpmz0cJ|passage=The big question is who gets what part of the party? Howard's angry, he'll get the '''angries'''.}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive|obsolete}} To [[anger]].
#* {{quote-book|en|title=The Cathechisme or Manner How to Instruct and Teach Children and Others in the Christian Faith.{{nb...|Appointed to Bee Read in All the Lands and Dominions of the Late Right and Mightie Prince, Fredericke Counte Palatine by the Rhine, One of the Electors of the Holy Empire, and Duke in  Bauier / Newly Translated out of Latin and Dutch into Englishe.}}|location=London|publisher={{...|Printed by}} Henrie Middleton, for Iohn Harison|year=1578|passage=Onely they that repent, and are verie ſorie that they haue '''angried''' God with their ſinnes, and yet truſt that they are forgiuẽ them for Chriſtes ſake, and that the reſt of their weakeneſſe and vnperfectnes is couered with his deth & paſſion, who alſo deſire to goe forwarde and growe more and more in holy life & conuerſation.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|author=[[w:John Stow|Iohn Stow]] (collector)|title=The Chronicles of England, from Brute vnto This Present Yeare of Christ 1580.|location=London|publisher={{...|Printed at London by}} Ralphe Newberie,{{nb...|at the assignement of Henrie Bynneman}}|year=1580|page=512|passage=The King ſent to the ''Londoners'' requeſting to borrowe of them one thouſande pounde, whiche they ſtoutely denyed, and alſo euil entreated, bette and néere hand ſlew a certain ''Lumbard'' that woulde haue lent the King the ſayde ſumme, which when the King heard he was maruellouſly '''angried''', and calling togither almoſt all the nobles of the lande, hée opened to them the malitiouſneſſe of the ''Londoners'', and cõplayned of theyr preſumption, the whyche noble men gaue counſell, that their inſolencie ſhoulde with ſpéede be oppreſſed, and theyr pride abated.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|author=William Biddulph|title=The Trauels of Certaine Englishmen into Africa, Asia, Troy, Bythinia, Thracia, and to the Blacke Sea.{{nb...|And into Syria, Cilicia, Pisidia, Mesopotamia, Damascus, Canaan, Galile, Samaria, Iudea, Palestina, Ierusalem, Iericho, and to the Red Sea: and to Sundry Other Places. Begunne in the Yeere of Iubile 1600. and by Some of Them Finished in This Yeere 1608. The Others Not Yet Returned. Very Profitable to the Help of Trauellers, and No Lesse Delightfull to All Persons Who Take Pleasure to Heare of the Manners, Gouernement, Religion, and Customes of Forraine and Heathen Countries.}}|location=London|publisher={{...|Printed by}} Th. Haueland, for W. Aspley,{{nb...|and are to bee sold at his shop in Paules Church-yard, at the signe of the Parrot}}|year=1609|pages=49–50|passage=For when the ''Arabians'' being offended with ''Heraclius'' for denying them their pay, and for his religion had ſeuered themſelues from him, ''Mahomet'' ioyned himſelfe to the '''angried''' ſouldiers, and ſtirred vp their minds againſt their Emperour, and encouraged them in their defection.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|author=Iohn Iackson|title=The Soule Is Immortall: or, Certaine Discourses Defending the Immortalitie of the Soule; Against the Limmes of Sathan: to Wit, Saduces, Anabaptistes, Atheists, and Such Like of the Hellish Crue of Aduersaries|location=London|publisher={{...|Imprinted at London by}} W. W. for Robert Boulton{{nb...|dwelling in Smithfield neere Long-lane}}|year=1611|page=173|passage=For verily the common ſort (O ''Socratus'' my friende,) is ingratefull, full of mockes and ſcornes, vaine, ſoone '''angried''', cruel, enuious, rude, heaped full of troubles and trifles: and whoſeuer doth familiarly acquaint himſelfe with them, & conuerſe amongſt them, doth at the length, become farre more miſerable then they be themſelues.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|author=R[obert] V[ase]|title=Ionah’s Contestation about His Gourd. In a Sermon Deliuered at Pauls Crosse. Septemb. 19. 1624.|location=London|publisher={{...|Printed by}} I. It was a milde ſaying of ''Auguſtus'' the Emperour to one of his ſouldiers deſirous to be diſmiſſed his armie, but wanting a iuſt and honeſt excuſe to his friends at his returne home, ſay, ſaith the Emperour, that I have '''angried''' thee.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|author=[[[w:Richard Smith (bishop)|Richard Smith]]]|title=A Conference of the Catholike and Protestante Doctrine with the Expresse Words of Holie Scripture. Which Is the Second Parte of the Prudentiall Balance of Religion. VVherein Is Clearely Shewed, That in More than 260. #* {{quote-book|en|author=[[w:Philip Ayres (poet)|Philip Ayres]]|title=Mythologia Ethica: or, Three Centuries of Æsopian Fables. In English Prose.
